query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of boron into eutectic high-entropy alloys will cause boron atoms to preferentially segregate to the internal boundaries of the dual-phase lamellar colonies. This enhanced interfacial cohesion will both reinforce the load-bearing interfaces (increasing tensile strength) and suppress microcrack nucleation (improving room‐temperature tensile ductility) compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that contain numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition (trace boron doping) during alloy synthesis to promote boron segregation at the internal boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under identical processing conditions; the boron level must be optimized to ensure segregation at the boundaries without forming deleterious secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial cohesion at the lamellar colony boundaries due to boron segregation.
generation.mechanism: Trace boron atoms, when added in controlled amounts, are expected to segregate to the internal boundaries of the lamellar microstructure, thereby increasing the boundary cohesive energy. This reinforcement delays the initiation and propagation of microcracks during tensile deformation, enabling a simultaneous increase in tensile strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the boron-doped variant will exhibit higher tensile strength and greater elongation (ductility) under room-temperature tensile tests.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that typically shows a trade-off between strength and ductility due to microcrack initiation at weak boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are contingent on the boron doping level being sufficiently low to promote interfacial segregation without triggering the formation of harmful secondary phases or compromising other mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in strength and ductility remains uncertain, as it will depend on the exact boron concentration, alloy composition, and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of the eutectic high-entropy alloy with an optimized trace boron doping level and a control set without boron. Ensure that both sets undergo identical casting and thermomechanical processing. Subject both sets to standardized room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Fractographic analysis to assess microcrack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both tensile strength and ductility (or if they perform worse) compared to the undoped control, the hypothesis that trace boron doping improves both properties will be falsified.

Metallurgists have dreamed to fabricate alloys with ultrahigh tensile strength and excellent ductility (>30% plastic strain) simultaneously at one temperature, even better over a wider temperature range (). The mechanical response of alloys is remarkably dependent on the service temperature, and it is extremely difficult for a specific alloy to have excellent strength-ductility combinations over a wide temperature range. Advanced structural materials must have a high damage tolerance without premature fracture. The emergence of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) in recent years presents an unconventional concept and approach as compared with conventional alloy designing (). These HEAs and MEAs are a new class of materials composed of multiprincipal elements with the possible potential for a wide range of property combinations (, ). The face-centered cubic (fcc) CrCoNi family of HEAs is characterized by their low yield strength at room temperature, while the body-centered cubic (bcc) refractory element family of HEAs exhibits insufficient ductility (). frame.system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys featuring dual‐phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that act as microcrack nucleation sites during room‐temperature tensile deformation.
frame.goal: To improve both the strength and the room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the current unmodified lamellar-colony microstructure.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing and previous microstructural-design strategies typically increase strength at the expense of ductility, and have not eliminated the inherent room-temperature brittleness caused by microcrack initiation at the internal boundaries.
root_cause_cues: conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility
constraints: The intervention must be a single, standalone modification
It must be effective specifically in the room-temperature tensile regime
The improvement should not compromise other mechanical properties
frame.regime: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions where microcrack initiation at internal boundaries determines ductility and strength.
prior_attempts: Various microstructural-design and processing strategies (e.g., altering lamellar spacing, phase fraction adjustments, heat treatment variations) that typically result in a trade-off between strength and ductility
Conventional processing methods that improve strength by refining microstructure, yet at the cost of a more brittle response and reduced tensile ductility
frame.hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition that preferentially segregates to and strengthens the internal boundaries—such as trace boron doping—can enhance interfacial cohesion and reduce microcrack nucleation. This intervention is expected to simultaneously improve tensile strength (by reinforcing the load-bearing boundaries) and increase ductility (by delaying crack initiation and propagation) compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline. The boundary condition for this effect is that the doping level must be optimized to ensure boundary segregation without forming deleterious secondary phases. Prior evidence from steels and other high-entropy alloys indicates that trace boron additions can enhance grain-boundary cohesion and delay fracture. An experiment to falsify this hypothesis would involve fabricating sets of alloys with and without boron doping under identical processing conditions, then subjecting them to room-temperature tensile tests. A failure to observe any concurrent improvement in both strength and ductility—relative to the baseline—would invalidate the hypothesis.
